_comment: Real plants, with an append-only status history. This is the file the watch agent's
second channel writes to, and the reason its shape is strict.
Schema and vocabularies: sources/sector_map.py. Gate: sources/check_sector_schema.py.
STATUS_HISTORY IS APPEND-ONLY AND EVERY ENTRY CARRIES A SOURCE. A status that changed
without a link is a status nobody can check, and the history is the one part of this
layer that is meant to be read as a record rather than as an analysis. Entries are in
date order and the last one equals `status`; the gate fails on either being untrue,
because a header and a timeline that disagree put two different facts on one page.
A SHORT HISTORY IS HONEST. Several of these projects start their history at the event
this repository first sourced — the grant, the groundbreaking — rather than at their
announcement, because no primary source for the earlier event has been read yet. The
file records what was verified, not what is likely to have happened.
`public_funding.measure` points at the register measure that IS the programme, and carries
`measure_note` saying how tight the fit is. The Innovation Fund lines are the live case: the
grants were awarded under the Fund as it stands (Art. 10a(8) of the ETS Directive), while the
register knows the Fund through the revision's Art. 10cb, which re-establishes it. Linking them
is what lets the money model total public support for the sector; the note is what stops the
link from being read as a claim that the award was made under the proposed article.

`public_funding` used to sit on each row. It moved to data/transition/funding.json, where capital allocation is a node with edges out of it: one Innovation Fund call finances several projects, and a field on the recipient could only say so by repeating itself once per recipient. The project keeps a rollup and the rollup is DERIVED — computed from the funding rows wherever it is shown, never stored back here.
`shared`: OPTIONAL, AND ONLY EVER TRUE. A project is claimed by the ecosystem whose
product it makes (page specifications §4.2), and two claims on one project fail the
build — a boundary drawn twice is a boundary somebody has to redraw. A CO2 store or a
hydrogen pipeline serving three industries is the exception the rule needs, and it
says so with "shared": true and a note giving the industries it serves. A plant making
one product never carries it.
WHERE IT IS, IN THE SAME BREATH AS WHAT IT IS. `location` is a LIST of sites, because a
project is not always at one place: the ArcelorMittal row covers Bremen and
Eisenhüttenstadt, and a single point for it would put a fact on the map that is half
wrong. One site is the ordinary case and the list of one says so honestly.
Every site carries {site, lat, lon, precision, retrieved_date, source, confidence} — the
parameter discipline, applied to a coordinate. `precision` is `plant` for a works and
`site` for a store or a terminal; `town` is in the vocabulary only so that the gate can
name what it is refusing. A town centroid is not a plant location: it would draw a mark
a reader would take for the works, several kilometres from the works. The coordinates
are read off OpenStreetMap features that carry the operator's or the works' own name,
which is a source that states a position rather than an address somebody geocoded in
their head; where a company publishes the plant address, `address` records it beside the
point. `confidence` is `secondary` throughout: OpenStreetMap is a third party reporting
somebody else's site.
`role` says what kind of place it is, and the map draws each differently. `plant` is the
default and is omitted; `storage` is a permitted or proposed geological store. A store is
in this file rather than in one of its own because it is what this file already says it
is — a real installation with an append-only status history — and because the exception
the `shared` flag was written for is exactly a CO2 store serving several industries.
`storage` IS REQUIRED ON EVERY CAPTURE PROJECT and has two shapes. Either it names the
project id of the store the tonne reaches, with the source that names it; or it says
`"unresolved": true` with a note saying how far the chain is actually specified. Five of
the nine capture projects here are unresolved, and that is the finding, not a hole: a
kiln with a capture unit and nowhere to send the CO2 is the thing the sector page exists
to show. An unresolved row still carries a source, because "nobody has said" is itself a
claim about a document somebody read.

source.verbatim: The CO₂ is transported via ships from Heidelberg Materials' cement factory in Brevik. The CO₂ is then offloaded and transported through a 100-kilometer pipeline and injected into the Aurora reservoir under the seabed of the North Sea.

status_history.note: Mechanical completion reached on schedule.
Opening of the facility; the first industrial-scale capture plant in the cement industry.

source.verbatim: The captured CO₂ is intended to be transported to the North Sea and permanently stored offshore in secure storage facilities at depths between 1000 and 3000 metres.

status_history.note: Work on Termoli and Kaiserslautern put on hold from May 2024 while ACC weighed a move to lithium iron phosphate.

Status unchanged, and the sources disagree about what happened. The Italian union UILM said on 7 February 2026 that the project was 'definitively shelved'. ACC's own words are that the conditions for restarting the projects 'are unlikely to be met', and that it has begun a 'constructive dialogue' with unions about potential discontinuation. Under the standing press ruling the status follows the project's own sources, which describe a condition and a talks process rather than a decision, so it stays paused.

status_history.note: Northvolt AB, Northvolt Ett AB, Northvolt Labs AB, Northvolt Revolt AB and Northvolt Systems AB filed for bankruptcy in Sweden on 12 March 2025. A court-appointed trustee was to determine the future of the production facilities. The history starts here because it is the first event sourced on this row; the site produced cells from 2021.

Lyten completed the acquisition of Northvolt Ett, Ett Expansion and Northvolt Labs and said it would begin the restart process immediately, with commercial cells planned for the second half of 2026. The site did not change status: it is the owner that changed, and the restart had not happened when this was recorded.
